questions.explanation: Profit = (P x Q) - [FC + (UVC x Q)] = ($120 x 600) - [$32,000 + ($40 x 600)] = $72,000 - $56,000 = $16,000. Equivalently, 200 frames beyond the 400-frame BEP x $80 contribution = $16,000. $48,000 forgets the fixed costs.

questions.stem: The owner of a new Edmonton bakery asks, 'How many loaves do I need to sell before I stop losing money?' Which technique answers this directly?
questions.explanation: Break-even analysis examines the relationship between total revenue and total cost to find the quantity at which TR = TC - where losses end and profit begins. Price elasticity tells how quantity responds to price, not how many units cover costs.

questions.stem: If a firm's fixed costs rise while its price and unit variable cost stay the same, its break-even point rises, because more units are needed to cover the larger fixed cost.
questions.explanation: True. BEP = FC / (P - UVC); fixed cost is the numerator, so raising it raises the BEP while the contribution per unit stays the same. For example, $32,000 / $80 = 400 frames becomes $40,000 / $80 = 500 frames.

questions.stem: Which statement about a break-even chart is NOT correct?
options: The total cost line begins at the level of fixed costs
The area between the lines to the right of the break-even point represents profit
At the break-even point, total revenue equals total cost
The total revenue line begins at the level of fixed costs
questions.explanation: Total revenue starts at zero (no sales, no revenue); it is the total COST line that starts at the fixed-cost level, because fixed costs exist even at zero output. Profit lies beyond the BEP, where TR exceeds TC.

questions.stem: Kestrel Cycles sets its new e-bike's price mainly by checking what rival brands charge and pricing just below them. Which group of pricing approaches is Kestrel using?
questions.explanation: Competition-oriented approaches focus on what competitors are doing rather than on demand, cost or profit; pricing just below rivals is below-market pricing. Demand-oriented approaches start from customers' tastes and preferences instead.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a demand-oriented pricing approach?
questions.explanation: Target return-on-sales pricing is PROFIT-oriented, along with target profit and target ROI. Bundle, odd-even and yield management are all demand-oriented, as are skimming, penetration, prestige and target pricing.

questions.stem: Target pricing and target profit pricing sound alike. Which statement correctly places them in Figure 9-2?
options: Target pricing is demand-oriented; target profit pricing is profit-oriented
Target pricing is cost-oriented; target profit pricing is demand-oriented
questions.explanation: Target pricing starts with the price consumers will pay and works backward, so it is demand-oriented. Target profit pricing solves for the price that yields a specific dollar profit, so it is profit-oriented, along with target return on sales and target ROI.

questions.stem: _____ approaches to pricing emphasize factors underlying expected customer tastes and preferences.
questions.explanation: Demand-oriented approaches (skimming, penetration, prestige, odd-even, target, bundle, yield management) weigh customer tastes and preferences. Competition-oriented approaches instead focus on what competitors are doing.

questions.stem: Why does Figure 9-2 describe its four groups of approaches as ways to select only an APPROXIMATE price level?
options: Because the Competition Bureau must approve the final price
Because the list price, special adjustments and ongoing monitoring still refine the price
Because the approaches apply only to new products
Because costs cannot be known until the product is sold
questions.explanation: Selecting an approximate price level is only Step 1. The firm still sets the list or quoted price (Step 2), makes special adjustments such as discounts, allowances and geographic adjustments (Step 3), and monitors and adjusts prices (Step 4). No regulator approves ordinary prices.

questions.stem: The manufacturer of a new variety of fat-free ice cream needs to determine a pricing strategy for its new product. Which of the following conditions would suggest using a skimming pricing strategy for the tasty fat-free ice cream?
options: The ice cream market is highly conservative
A large portion of the market has inelastic demand for fat-free ice cream, over a fairly broad range of prices
Economies of scale in production are substantial
Retailers are willing to pay for new brands of premium ice cream in an extremely overcrowded category
questions.explanation: Skimming works when enough customers are price-insensitive - inelastic demand over a broad range of prices - because they weigh the new product's price, quality and ability to satisfy their needs against substitutes. Substantial economies of scale favour PENETRATION pricing, since lower unit costs reward high volume.

questions.stem: H&G Co. Ltd. has used a high initial price for its newly launched cellphones. The company hopes to recover its research and development costs with this pricing. This is an example of a:
questions.explanation: A high initial price used to help recover research and development costs is price skimming. Prestige pricing also uses a high price, but to attract status-conscious buyers permanently - not as a launch tactic for recovering R&D.

questions.stem: Which scenario describes skimming rather than prestige pricing?
options: A Swiss watch brand keeps prices high year after year because lower prices would hurt its exclusive image
A designer handbag maker found that cutting prices reduced sales
A gaming-console maker launches at $899, planning price cuts as competitors release rival consoles
A luxury vodka is priced well above other vodkas to appeal to status-conscious buyers
questions.explanation: Skimming sets a high INITIAL price on a new product and lowers it over time as competitors enter. The other three keep prices high permanently to attract status-conscious buyers - prestige pricing, where cutting price can reduce demand.

questions.stem: Which condition does NOT favour a skimming strategy for a new product?
options: The high price signals high quality to buyers
Competitors cannot enter quickly because of patents
Unit costs drop sharply as production volume grows
Enough buyers are relatively insensitive to price
questions.explanation: When unit costs fall sharply with volume (economies of scale), a low price that builds volume pays off - a PENETRATION condition. Skimming favours price-insensitive early buyers, a quality signal and barriers that keep competitors out.

questions.stem: BioClear has a patented water filter that rivals cannot copy for several years. Research shows a sizable group of health-conscious buyers will pay almost any price, and production costs will not drop much with volume. Which initial pricing approach fits best?
questions.explanation: All the skimming conditions are present: price-insensitive buyers (an inelastic segment), a barrier to entry (the patent) and little cost advantage from volume. Penetration would suit price-sensitive buyers and strong economies of scale - neither is present.

questions.stem: When Pixel Play launched its new handheld game console, it priced it well below rival systems to appeal immediately to the mass market and build a large user base quickly. This is:
questions.explanation: Penetration pricing sets a low initial price on a new product to appeal immediately to the mass market (the instructor's example is the Nintendo Wii U). Loss-leader pricing cuts the price of an existing item to pull traffic toward other products - not a new-product launch strategy.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions makes penetration pricing most attractive?
options: Price-insensitive buyers and high barriers to entry
Price-sensitive buyers, unit costs that fall with volume, and a low price that discourages competitors
A product bought mainly as a status symbol
A fixed, perishable capacity such as hotel rooms
questions.explanation: Penetration works when many buyers are price-sensitive (elastic demand), economies of scale lower unit costs as volume grows, and the low price discourages competitors. Price-insensitive buyers plus entry barriers describe skimming; perishable capacity suits yield management.

questions.stem: Which scenario is penetration pricing rather than loss-leader pricing?
options: A new meal-kit company enters Ontario at $5 per meal, far below rivals, to build a subscriber base quickly
A Calgary supermarket sells butter at $2.99, below its usual price, to draw shoppers in
A hardware chain sells snow shovels below their customary price on the first snowy weekend to boost store traffic
An electronics store advertises a Black Friday TV doorbuster to fill the store
questions.explanation: Penetration is a low INITIAL price on a NEW product to win the mass market. The others cut prices on existing items to attract traffic in hopes shoppers buy other products - loss-leader pricing, a competition-oriented approach.

questions.stem: SnapCharge is launching a phone charger in a market full of price-sensitive buyers. Its factory's unit cost will drop sharply as volume rises, and it wants to discourage rivals from entering. What initial price should it set?
options: A high initial price to recover R&D, lowered later
A low initial price to win the mass market quickly
A price ending in an even number to signal quality
A price set by tradition for the category
questions.explanation: Elastic demand, economies of scale and a desire to deter competitors are the classic penetration conditions, so a low initial price fits. A high initial price lowered later is skimming, which needs price-insensitive buyers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a condition favouring penetration pricing?
options: Many segments of the market are price-sensitive
Unit costs fall as production experience accumulates
A low price discourages competitors from entering
A large segment has inelastic demand over a broad range of prices
questions.explanation: A large segment with inelastic demand is a SKIMMING condition - those buyers will pay a high initial price. Penetration needs price-sensitive (elastic) buyers, economies of scale or experience, and a low price that keeps competitors out.

questions.stem: Aurelia Perfumes cut the price of its signature fragrance from $240 to $150 and was shocked when sales dropped. Buyers had valued the high price as a mark of exclusivity. Which approach should Aurelia have stuck with?
questions.explanation: Prestige pricing sets a high price so status-conscious consumers will buy; for these goods, lowering the price can reduce demand. Penetration and below-market pricing rely on low prices to win volume - exactly what backfired.

questions.stem: For a prestige product, why can a price cut REDUCE the quantity demanded?
options: Because fixed costs rise when price falls
Because competitors immediately match the lower price
Because the demand curve bends backward: a lower price makes the product less attractive to status-conscious buyers
questions.explanation: Prestige goods have a demand curve that bends backward over part of its range: a lower price signals less status, so fewer people want the product. Inelastic demand would mean quantity barely changes - not that it falls when price falls.

questions.stem: Luxe Motors prices its sports cars 20% above competitors' average price, deliberately using that market price as its benchmark. Which approach is this, as opposed to prestige pricing?
questions.explanation: Using competitors' market price as a benchmark and pricing above it is above-market pricing, a competition-oriented approach (the instructor's example is the iPhone 17). Prestige pricing is demand-oriented: the high price is set to attract status-conscious buyers, not measured against rivals' prices.

questions.stem: _____ pricing involves setting a high price so that quality- or status-conscious consumers will be attracted to the product and buy it.
questions.explanation: That is the definition of prestige pricing. Skimming also uses a high price, but only initially for a new product, typically to recover R&D before the price is lowered over time.

questions.stem: Prestige pricing sets a high initial price that the firm plans to lower as competitors enter the market.
questions.explanation: False. A high initial price planned to fall as competitors enter describes SKIMMING. Prestige pricing keeps the price high permanently because the high price is part of the product's status appeal; lowering it can actually reduce demand.

questions.stem: Deliberately adjusting the composition and features of a product to achieve the price consumers are willing to pay is called:
questions.explanation: Target pricing estimates the price consumers will pay, then works backward to design and cost the product. Target profit pricing instead solves the profit equation for the price that yields a specific dollar profit.

questions.stem: Northwind Furniture learns that university students will pay about $199 for a desk. Its engineers then choose particleboard, a flat-pack design and fewer drawers so the desk can be made for $110 and still sell profitably at $199. This is:
questions.explanation: Target pricing starts with the price consumers are willing to pay and works backward, adjusting the product's composition and features to hit the needed cost. Cost-plus does the reverse - it starts with the cost and adds an amount on top.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes target pricing from target profit pricing?
options: Target pricing adds a fixed percentage to cost; target profit pricing benchmarks against competitors
They are two names for the same profit-oriented approach
Target pricing starts from what consumers will pay and designs backward; target profit pricing solves for the price that yields a set dollar profit
Target pricing is profit-oriented; target profit pricing is demand-oriented
questions.explanation: Target pricing is demand-oriented - the consumer's acceptable price comes first and the product is engineered to fit. Target profit pricing is profit-oriented - it plugs a dollar profit goal, costs and volume into the profit equation and solves for price.

questions.stem: In target pricing, what is the FIRST step?
options: Total the product's costs and add a markup
Estimate the price consumers are willing to pay
questions.explanation: Target pricing begins by estimating the price consumers will pay, then works backward through the needed margins to the cost the product must be designed to. Totalling costs first is the cost-oriented logic (standard markup, cost-plus).

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT characteristic of target pricing?
options: The product's features may be changed to hit a cost
It begins with the firm's total unit cost and adds a set amount
It starts with an estimate of what consumers will pay
questions.explanation: Beginning with total unit cost and adding a set amount is cost-plus pricing (cost-oriented). Target pricing begins with consumers' acceptable price and adjusts the product to meet a cost that makes that price work.

questions.stem: Maple Fibre offers home internet, TV and a mobile line for $120 a month, compared with $155 if bought separately. This is:
questions.explanation: Bundle pricing markets two or more products in a single package price. A quantity discount rewards buying MORE of the same product, not combining different products.

questions.stem: Why do fast-food chains use bundle pricing for value meals?
options: Buyers see the package as a better deal than buying items separately, and the chain sells more items per order
It lets them charge different prices to different customers for the same item
It is required by the Competition Act
It allows them to recover R&D costs quickly
questions.explanation: Bundle pricing gives buyers perceived savings on a package and lets the seller move more products per sale. Charging different buyers different prices for the same item is a flexible-price policy, not bundling.

questions.stem: Which of the following is bundle pricing rather than yield management?
options: An airline charges $129 for a Tuesday seat and $389 for a Friday seat on the same route
A ski resort sells a lift ticket, rental skis and a lesson together for one price
A hotel raises room rates as occupancy for a weekend climbs
A theatre charges more for seats to a nearly sold-out Saturday show
questions.explanation: Bundle pricing combines two or more products (lift ticket, rentals, lesson) into one package price. The other three vary the price of the same fixed capacity by date or demand - yield management.

questions.stem: _____ pricing is the marketing of two or more products in a single package price.
questions.explanation: Bundle pricing combines products into one package price (e.g., a value meal). Loss-leader pricing, by contrast, prices ONE item below its customary price to attract traffic.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of bundle pricing?
options: A car dealer includes winter tires, mats and remote start in one package price
A cafe sells a coffee-and-muffin combo for $5
A grocer gives 10% off any single order over $200
A software firm sells three apps together for one suite price
questions.explanation: Ten percent off a large single order is a noncumulative quantity DISCOUNT, a Step 3 adjustment. The other three sell two or more products together for a single package price - bundle pricing.

questions.stem: Peak View Hotel in Banff charges $189 for a standard room on a quiet November Tuesday and $549 for the same room on a ski-season Saturday, adjusting rates to earn the most from its 120 rooms. This is:
questions.explanation: Yield management charges different prices to maximize revenue for a set amount of capacity at a given time - the 120 rooms are fixed and an unsold night is lost forever. Skimming is a high initial price on a new product that falls over time, not a rate that moves with demand for fixed capacity.

questions.stem: Yield management pricing is the marketing of two or more products in a single package price.
questions.explanation: False. That describes bundle pricing. Yield management pricing is charging different prices to maximize revenue for a set amount of capacity at any given time, as airlines and hotels do.

questions.stem: Which scenario is yield management pricing, rather than flexible pricing based on the individual buyer?
options: A transit system charges seniors and students lower fares than adults
A car dealer negotiates a different price with each buyer
An airline raises fares on a flight as its remaining seats fill up
A furniture store lets salespeople haggle with customers
questions.explanation: Yield management varies price with demand for a FIXED capacity at a given time (the flight's remaining seats). The others vary price by the individual BUYER - age-based fares and haggling are flexible-price policies.

questions.stem: Why is yield management especially suited to airlines and hotels?
options: Their capacity is fixed, and a seat or room left unsold on a given date can never be sold later
Their products are commodities sold in pure competition
Their costs are almost entirely variable
Customary prices in these industries cannot be changed
questions.explanation: Yield management maximizes revenue from a set amount of capacity at a given time; an empty seat after departure is revenue lost forever, so varying prices to fill capacity pays off. These are differentiated services, not commodities, and their costs are largely fixed.

questions.stem: For which business would yield management pricing be LEAST useful?
options: A Calgary concert venue with 2,000 seats per show
A ferry with a fixed number of car spaces per sailing
A canned-soup manufacturer that can store unsold inventory
A Whistler ski lodge with 60 rooms
questions.explanation: Yield management fits fixed, time-bound capacity that perishes if unsold - seats, car spaces and rooms. A soup maker can store unsold cans and sell them later, so there is no perishable capacity to manage.

questions.stem: Nature's Taste, a manufacturer of floral jellies made from pansies, honeysuckle, and wisteria, prices its jellies by adding 30 percent to the cost of everything that goes into making the jellies including salaries, jars, sugar, and pectin. Which of the following pricing methods is being used here?
questions.explanation: Adding a set percentage (30%) to cost is standard markup pricing; manufacturers commonly express markup as a percentage of cost - (price - cost) / cost. Target return-on-sales pricing would set price to earn profit equal to a percentage of SALES, not cost.

questions.stem: Trailhead Outfitters sells a jacket for $75 that cost it $60. Expressed as a percentage of the SELLING PRICE, what is the markup?
questions.explanation: Markup on price = (price - cost) / price = ($75 - $60) / $75 = $15 / $75 = 20%. 25% is the markup on COST ($15 / $60), and 80% is cost as a percentage of price (Figure 9-3).

questions.stem: A Quebec maple-syrup maker's cost to produce a case is $50, and it sells the case to distributors for $80. Expressed as a percentage of COST, what is the markup?
questions.explanation: Markup on cost = (price - cost) / cost = ($80 - $50) / $50 = $30 / $50 = 60%. 37.5% is the markup on PRICE ($30 / $80) - the base matters. Manufacturers often express markup on cost; retailers on price.

questions.stem: Bloom & Co., a Winnipeg flower shop, buys a bouquet for $30 and wants a 40% markup on the SELLING PRICE. What should the selling price be?
questions.explanation: When markup is on price, price is 100% and cost is 100% - 40% = 60% of price. Price = $30 / 0.60 = $50.00 (check: $20 markup / $50 = 40%). $42.00 applies 40% to COST ($30 x 1.4), which is only a 28.6% markup on price.

questions.stem: A manufacturer uses a 50% markup on cost. A retail buyer asks what that markup equals when expressed as a percentage of the selling price. What is the correct answer?
questions.explanation: Assume cost = $100. A 50% markup on cost adds $50, so price = $150. Markup on price = $50 / $150 = 33.3% (formula: 0.50 / (1 + 0.50)). 66.7% converts the other way - it is the markup on cost that matches a 40% markup on price.

questions.stem: Which situation is standard markup pricing rather than cost-plus pricing?
options: A contractor bills a city for a library's total construction cost plus a $250,000 fee
A consulting firm charges a government department its actual costs plus 10% on a one-time project
A Calgary drugstore adds the same 35% to the cost of every item in its cosmetics department
A defence supplier is paid its audited costs plus a fixed fee for a custom radar system
questions.explanation: Standard markup adds a fixed percentage to the cost of ALL items in a product class - typical of retailers. The other three total the cost of a specific job or contract and add a specific amount or percentage: cost-plus pricing, common in construction and government contracts.

questions.stem: When markup is expressed relative to selling price, the selling price is always treated as 100 percent.
questions.explanation: True. In Figure 9-3 the $75 selling price = 100%, the $60 cost = 80% and the $15 markup = 20% of price. When markup is relative to cost, cost becomes the 100% base instead, so the same $15 is 25%.

questions.stem: Ironbridge Construction agrees to build a new fire hall for the City of Lethbridge. The city will pay Ironbridge's total project costs, whatever they turn out to be, plus a fixed fee of $300,000. This pricing method is:
questions.explanation: Cost-plus pricing sums the total cost of providing the product or service and adds a specific amount - common in construction and government contracts. Standard markup applies the same percentage to the cost of all items in a product class, as retailers do.

questions.stem: Polaris Engineering will design a custom water-treatment system for an Alberta town on a cost-plus basis: total costs plus 8%. If the project's total costs come to $2,400,000, what will the town pay?
questions.explanation: Cost-plus = total cost + the specified percentage of cost = $2,400,000 + (0.08 x $2,400,000) = $2,400,000 + $192,000 = $2,592,000. $2,208,000 subtracts the 8% instead of adding it.

questions.stem: Cost-plus pricing and standard markup pricing both start with cost. What best distinguishes cost-plus pricing?
options: It adds a specific amount to the total cost of a particular job or contract; standard markup adds one percentage to a whole product class
It starts with consumer demand, while standard markup starts with cost
It is profit-oriented, while standard markup is cost-oriented
It is used mainly by grocery retailers, while standard markup is used mainly in government contracts
questions.explanation: Both are cost-oriented, but cost-plus totals the cost of a specific job (construction, government contracts, services) and adds a specific amount, while standard markup adds a fixed percentage to every item in a class (retailers, manufacturers). Claiming grocery retailers rely on cost-plus reverses who typically uses which approach.

questions.stem: _____ pricing involves summing the total unit cost of providing a product or service and adding a specific amount to the cost to arrive at a price.
questions.explanation: That is cost-plus pricing - total unit cost plus a specific amount. Standard markup is similar but applies a fixed percentage to the cost of all items in a product class rather than to a specific job.

questions.stem: Cost-plus pricing would be LEAST likely to be used by which organization?
options: A construction firm building a hospital wing
An engineering firm on a custom government contract
A grocery chain pricing 30,000 everyday items
A consulting firm billing a one-time project
questions.explanation: A grocer pricing thousands of items would use standard markup (a set percentage on the cost of all items in a class). Cost-plus is common in construction, government contracts and services, where each job's total cost is summed and a specific amount added.

questions.stem: Charlie Tuna Inc. sells five-pound packages of ocean tuna. Its variable cost per package is $40, and its fixed cost is $410,000. It wants a target profit of $42,000 on a volume of 21,000 packages. What should it charge for a five-pound package of tuna?
questions.explanation: Target profit pricing: Profit = (P x Q) - [FC + (UVC x Q)]. $42,000 = (P x 21,000) - [$410,000 + ($40 x 21,000)], so 21,000P = $42,000 + $410,000 + $840,000 = $1,292,000 and P = $61.52. $40 is only the variable cost, which would cover neither fixed costs nor profit.

questions.stem: Fjord Paddles has fixed costs of $150,000 and a unit variable cost of $12 per paddle. It expects to sell 20,000 paddles and wants a target profit of $50,000. What price should it set?
questions.explanation: P = (Target profit + FC + UVC x Q) / Q = ($50,000 + $150,000 + $12 x 20,000) / 20,000 = $440,000 / 20,000 = $22.00. $19.50 covers costs but leaves out the $50,000 profit; $10.00 forgets the variable cost per paddle.

questions.stem: Ridgeline Brewing's owners tell the marketing manager: 'Price our new lager so we make exactly $250,000 in profit this year on the volume we expect to sell.' Which approach is being requested?
questions.explanation: Setting an annual target of a specific DOLLAR amount of profit is target profit pricing. Target return on sales would express the goal as a percentage of sales revenue, and target pricing starts from the price consumers will pay.

questions.stem: Which goal calls for target profit pricing rather than target return-on-investment pricing?
options: Earn 15% on the $2 million invested in the new plant
Earn profit equal to 10% of sales revenue
Earn a 25% markup on cost on every unit
questions.explanation: A specific dollar amount ($180,000) is a target profit goal. A percentage of investment is target ROI, a percentage of sales is target return on sales, and a percentage added to cost is standard markup.

questions.stem: Charlie Tuna calculated a price of $61.52 assuming it would sell 21,000 packages (fixed cost $410,000; variable cost $40 per package). If it actually sells only 15,000 packages at that price, what happens and why?
options: It still earns $42,000, because the price already includes the target profit
It misses the target and loses money, because the price depended on an accurate demand estimate to cover fixed costs
It earns more than $42,000, because variable costs fall with lower volume
Its fixed costs fall in proportion to the lower volume, so profit is unchanged
questions.explanation: Profit-oriented approaches depend on accurate estimates of demand. At 15,000 packages: TR = $61.52 x 15,000 = $922,800; TC = $410,000 + ($40 x 15,000) = $1,010,000, a loss of $87,200. Fixed costs do not shrink with volume, so the shortfall hits profit directly.

questions.stem: Cascade Plastics invested $4 million in a new moulding line. Head office tells the marketing team to set prices that will earn an annual profit equal to 12% of that investment. Which approach is this?
questions.explanation: Setting price to achieve an annual target percentage return on investment is target ROI pricing. Target return on sales would base the percentage on sales revenue, and target profit pricing names a specific dollar amount.

questions.stem: Harbour Hats wants a profit equal to 20% of its sales revenue. Its fixed costs are $40,000, its unit variable cost is $30, and it expects to sell 2,000 hats. What price achieves this target return on sales?

Kodiak Tools invested $500,000 in new equipment and wants a 12% annual return on that investment. Its fixed costs are $100,000, its unit variable cost is $20, and expected volume is 10,000 units. What price should it charge?
questions.explanation: Target profit = 12% x $500,000 = $60,000. P = ($60,000 + $100,000 + $20 x 10,000) / 10,000 = $360,000 / 10,000 = $36.00. $30.00 only breaks even, and $86.00 wrongly adds the whole investment as if it were a cost to recover this year.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between target return-on-sales pricing and target return-on-investment pricing?
options: Return on sales sets profit as a percentage of sales revenue; ROI sets profit as a percentage of the money invested
Return on sales is demand-oriented; ROI is cost-oriented
Return on sales names a specific dollar profit; ROI uses a percentage
Return on sales is used only by manufacturers; ROI only by retailers
questions.explanation: Both are profit-oriented. Target return on sales expresses the profit goal as a percentage of sales volume (revenue); target ROI expresses it as a percentage of investment. A specific dollar profit is target profit pricing.

questions.stem: Setting a price to achieve a profit that is a specified percentage of the sales volume is called _____ pricing.
questions.explanation: Target return-on-sales pricing ties profit to a percentage of sales. Standard markup also uses a percentage, but it is added to COST (a cost-oriented approach) rather than being a profit target measured against sales.

questions.stem: SweetSpot Vending has charged $2.00 for its chocolate bars for years, because that price is set by tradition and is what vending-machine customers expect to pay. This is:
questions.explanation: Customary pricing sets a price based on tradition, a standardized channel of distribution or other competitive factors - vending items and candy bars are classic examples. Loss-leader pricing would deliberately price BELOW the customary price to pull traffic.

questions.stem: Zenith Audio wants its new headphones positioned as the premium choice. Its research shows competitors cluster around $250. Using a competition-oriented approach, what should Zenith do?
options: Price at $199 as a loss leader
Price above the $250 market price, using rivals' prices as the benchmark
Set the price to earn a 15% return on investment
questions.explanation: Above-market pricing uses the market price as a benchmark and deliberately prices above it to signal a premium position (the instructor's example is the iPhone 17). Standard markup and target ROI ignore competitors' prices; they are cost- and profit-oriented.

questions.stem: Which retailer is using below-market pricing rather than loss-leader pricing?
options: A grocer sells eggs at a deep discount for one weekend to draw shoppers into the store
A discount chain sets everyday prices about 5% under competitors' prices across its whole store
An electronics store advertises a Black Friday TV far below its usual price
A pharmacy features milk below its customary price to build traffic
questions.explanation: Below-market pricing is an ongoing positioning choice that uses competitors' market price as the benchmark (Walmart-style). The other three temporarily price a specific item below its customary price to attract traffic for other purchases - loss leaders.

questions.stem: Above-, at- or below-market pricing uses the _____ as the benchmark for setting a price.
options: price consumers are willing to pay
questions.explanation: Above-, at- or below-market pricing is competition-oriented: the 'market price' (what competitors charge) is the benchmark. Starting from consumers' willingness to pay would be target pricing, and starting from cost would be a cost-oriented approach.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a competition-oriented pricing approach?
questions.explanation: Prestige pricing is DEMAND-oriented - it targets status-conscious consumers. Customary, above/at/below-market and loss-leader pricing are the competition-oriented approaches, which focus on what competitors are doing.

questions.stem: Every Thursday, Bow Valley Foods advertises a 4 L jug of milk for $2.99, well below its customary $5.79, expecting shoppers who come for the milk to fill their carts with regularly priced items. This is:
questions.explanation: Loss-leader pricing deliberately sells a product below its customary price to attract attention and traffic, in hopes shoppers buy other products. Penetration pricing applies to a NEW product's low introductory price, not to a staple like milk.

questions.stem: Which of the following is loss-leader pricing rather than predatory pricing?
options: A big-box chain prices far below cost near a new independent rival until the rival closes, then raises prices
A Saskatoon grocer sells turkeys below their customary price before Thanksgiving to draw shoppers who will buy side dishes too
A dominant airline floods a new competitor's routes with below-cost fares to force it out
A cement maker undercuts a small rival's prices until the rival leaves the region
questions.explanation: Loss-leader pricing prices one item below its customary price to attract shoppers who will buy other products - a legal competition-oriented approach. The other three set very low prices to drive competitors out of business: predatory pricing, restricted by the Competition Act.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of loss-leader pricing?
options: To drive competitors out of business permanently
To reward buyers for paying their bills promptly
To attract store traffic in hopes customers buy other products as well
questions.explanation: Loss leaders draw attention and traffic; the retailer profits on the other items shoppers buy. Driving competitors out of business is predatory pricing, recovering R&D is skimming, and rewarding prompt payment is a cash discount.

questions.stem: Deliberately selling a product below its customary price to attract attention to it is called _____ pricing.
questions.explanation: Loss-leader pricing sells an item below its customary price to attract attention and traffic. Below-market pricing is an ongoing, store-wide positioning against competitors' prices, not a single item used to lure shoppers.

questions.stem: Which statement about loss-leader pricing is NOT correct?
options: Milk and eggs are common loss leaders
It is used to launch new products with a low introductory price
The retailer hopes shoppers will buy other products too
questions.explanation: A low introductory price on a new product is PENETRATION pricing. Loss leaders are usually familiar items (milk, eggs, Black Friday TVs) priced below their customary price to drive traffic - a competition-oriented approach.

questions.stem: In value-based pricing (Nagle/Holden), what is the FIRST element in the sequence?
questions.explanation: Value-based pricing runs Customers -> Value -> Price -> Cost -> Product, so it starts with customers. Cost-based pricing is the reverse and starts with the product.

questions.stem: In cost-based pricing, which element comes immediately AFTER price?
questions.explanation: Cost-based pricing runs Product -> Cost -> Price -> Value -> Customers: after setting the price, the firm must convince buyers of the value. In value-based pricing it is the reverse - value comes immediately BEFORE price.

questions.stem: Peak Tech designs a new trail camera, adds up its manufacturing and marketing costs, sets a price that covers them plus a margin, and then asks its ad agency to convince hunters the camera is worth it. Which pricing logic is this?
questions.explanation: Cost-based pricing follows Product -> Cost -> Price -> Value -> Customers: the product and costs come first, and value must be 'sold' afterward. Value-based (and target) pricing would start with what customers value and will pay.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts cost-based and value-based pricing?
options: Cost-based starts with the product and ends with customers; value-based starts with customers and ends with the product
Cost-based starts with customers; value-based starts with the product
Both sequences start with cost but end differently
questions.explanation: The two sequences are mirror images: cost-based = Product, Cost, Price, Value, Customers; value-based = Customers, Value, Price, Cost, Product. Value-based pricing does not ignore costs - cost comes after price, as the amount the firm can spend to deliver that value.

questions.stem: Why does value-based pricing begin with customers rather than with the product?
options: So the firm can guarantee a fixed margin over its unit cost
Because customers determine the firm's fixed costs
So the price reflects the value customers perceive, with costs and the product then designed to fit that price
So the firm never needs to consider competitors
questions.explanation: Pricing is the attempt to capture the value the marketing mix creates. Starting with customers and value means the price reflects what buyers perceive, and costs and the product are then held to what that price allows. Guaranteeing a margin over unit cost is the cost-based logic.

questions.stem: In setting a final price, which step comes immediately after 'set the list or quoted price'?
options: Make special adjustments to the list or quoted price
questions.explanation: The four steps are: (1) select an approximate price level, (2) set the list or quoted price, (3) make special adjustments - discounts, allowances, geographic adjustments, (4) monitor and adjust prices. Identifying constraints happens earlier in the pricing process, not within these four steps.

questions.stem: The first step in setting a final price is to set the list or quoted price.
questions.explanation: False. Step 1 is to select an approximate price level using one of the four approach buckets (demand-, cost-, profit- or competition-oriented). Setting the list or quoted price is Step 2.

questions.stem: Having already set a list price, Prairie Paint's sales manager now offers retailers 2/10 net 30 payment terms, a discount for orders placed before spring, and free freight to Saskatchewan stores. Which step of setting a final price is he working on?
options: Step 1: Select an approximate price level
Step 2: Set the list or quoted price
Step 3: Make special adjustments to the list or quoted price
questions.explanation: Discounts (cash, seasonal) and geographic adjustments (freight) are special adjustments made in Step 3. Step 2 is where the list price and the one-price vs flexible-price policy are set.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four steps in setting a final price?
options: Set the list or quoted price
Make special adjustments to the list or quoted price
questions.explanation: Identifying pricing objectives (and constraints) comes earlier in the pricing process. The four final-price steps are: select an approximate price level, set the list or quoted price, make special adjustments, and monitor and adjust prices.

questions.stem: Six months after launching its fitness app at $12.99 a month, Pulse Fitness sees subscriptions slip after a rival cuts its price to $8.99. Which step of setting a final price should Pulse now carry out?
options: Select an approximate price level for the first time
questions.explanation: Step 4 - monitor and adjust prices - responds to changes in competition, demand and costs after launch. Pricing is not 'set and forget'; Step 1 was completed at launch.

questions.stem: City transit services often offer different riders a unique price to ride based on age, employment, etc. This is an example of a _____ policy.
questions.explanation: A flexible-price policy sets different prices for products and services depending on individual buyers and purchase situations - here, riders' age or employment. A one-price policy would charge every rider the same fare.

questions.stem: At Clearwater Motors, every customer pays the posted sticker price - no haggling and no special deals - whether they are a first-time buyer or a returning customer. This is a:
questions.explanation: A one-price policy sets one price for all buyers of a product (no-haggle car brands and Walmart are examples). A flexible-price policy would let the price vary by buyer or situation, as in traditional dealer negotiation.

questions.stem: Which situation reflects a legal flexible-price policy rather than illegal price discrimination?
options: A manufacturer charges a large chain less than competing independent retailers for identical quantities, lessening competition
A Calgary museum charges students, seniors and adults different admission prices
A supplier secretly gives one distributor lower prices than its competing distributors for the same volume
A wholesaler charges two competing grocers different prices for the same order size, harming the smaller one
questions.explanation: Charging consumers different prices based on age or status is a legal flexible-price policy. Price discrimination involves charging COMPETING business buyers different prices for like quantities in a way that lessens competition - restricted under the Competition Act.

questions.stem: When a big concert ends in downtown Edmonton, a rideshare app's fares jump to 2.5 times normal for 30 minutes. What explains this dynamic pricing?
options: Prices are adjusted in real time based on demand
The app is using a one-price policy
The fare includes a uniform delivered charge
The app is practising customary pricing
questions.explanation: Dynamic pricing adjusts prices in real time based on demand - like Uber surge pricing - and is a form of flexible pricing. A one-price policy would keep the fare the same regardless of demand, and customary pricing keeps a traditional price.

questions.stem: _____ is the practice of adjusting prices in real time based on changes in demand.
questions.explanation: Dynamic pricing adjusts prices in real time as demand changes (for example, Uber surge pricing); it is a form of flexible pricing. Customary pricing does the opposite - it keeps a price fixed by tradition.

questions.stem: In the spring and early summer, before Canada Day, Molson Coors offers retailers a discount on Molson Canadian to see their product lead long-weekend sales. This is known as a:
questions.explanation: Seasonal discounts encourage buyers to buy an item or stock inventory earlier than their normal demand would require - retailers stock up before the Canada Day long weekend. A functional (trade) discount rewards resellers for performing marketing functions, not for timing.

questions.stem: Northern Supply invoices a Kelowna restaurant $5,000 on terms of 2/10 net 30. If the restaurant pays on day 8, how much does it pay?
questions.explanation: 2/10 net 30 means 2% off if paid within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due within 30 days. Paying on day 8 qualifies: $5,000 - (0.02 x $5,000) = $5,000 - $100 = $4,900. The full $5,000 applies only if it pays after day 10.

questions.stem: A manufacturer quotes a list price of $200 with a chain trade (functional) discount of 30/10/5 to wholesalers. What does a wholesaler pay?
questions.explanation: Chain discounts are applied one after another: $200 x 0.70 = $140; $140 x 0.90 = $126; $126 x 0.95 = $119.70. Adding the discounts together (45% off = $110) is the classic error - each discount applies to the already-reduced price.

questions.stem: A Red Deer cafe chain earns larger price reductions from its coffee roaster as its total purchases over the year add up, regardless of the size of any single order. This is a:
questions.explanation: Cumulative quantity discounts apply to total purchases over a period of time and encourage repeat buying and loyalty. Noncumulative quantity discounts are based on the size of a SINGLE order.

questions.stem: Crunchy Prairie Snacks gives Valley Fresh Grocers free cases of chips in return for running an end-of-aisle display and featuring the chips in its weekly flyer. This is a:
questions.explanation: Promotional allowances are cash payments or extra goods given to resellers for advertising or promoting the product; under the Competition Act they must be offered proportionally to all competing resellers. A functional (trade) discount rewards general channel functions such as warehousing and selling, not a specific promotion.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the discounts a seller might offer as a special adjustment to the list price?
questions.explanation: FOB origin pricing is a GEOGRAPHIC adjustment - it determines who pays freight and when title passes - not a discount. The four discounts are quantity, seasonal, trade (functional) and cash.

questions.stem: Discounts are reductions from list price that a seller gives a buyer as a reward for some favourable activity, such as paying promptly or buying in large quantities.
questions.explanation: True - this is the course definition of discounts. Each type rewards a different favourable activity: buying more (quantity), buying early (seasonal), performing marketing functions (trade or functional) or paying promptly (cash).

questions.stem: Free-on-board (FOB) origin pricing is a method of pricing where the:
options: title of goods remains with the manufacturer until sold to the ultimate consumer
title of goods passes to the buyer upon arrival at the final destination
title of goods passes to the buyer at the point of loading
price the seller sets includes all transportation costs
questions.explanation: FOB means 'free on board' some vehicle at some location: the seller pays to load the product, and title passes to the buyer at the point of loading, after which the buyer pays the freight. A price that includes all transportation costs describes uniform delivered pricing.

questions.stem: Prairie Gold Fertilizer quotes a Manitoba co-op a price at its Red Deer plant. Once the product is loaded onto the co-op's hired truck, the co-op owns it and pays the freight. This is:
questions.explanation: Under FOB origin pricing the buyer takes title at the point of loading and pays transportation from the seller's location. Uniform delivered pricing (and its variations such as single-zone and basing-point) builds freight into the seller's quoted price.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts FOB origin pricing with uniform delivered pricing?
options: Under FOB origin the seller pays freight; under uniform delivered the buyer pays
Both make distant buyers pay more than nearby buyers
Under uniform delivered pricing, title passes at the point of loading
Under FOB origin the buyer pays freight; under uniform delivered the price includes all transportation costs
questions.explanation: FOB origin: the buyer pays freight and takes title at the point of loading, so distant buyers pay more. Uniform delivered: the seller quotes a price that includes all transportation costs. Saying the seller pays freight under FOB origin reverses the roles.

questions.stem: Maple Lane Books, an online retailer in Toronto, charges every customer in Canada the same delivered price, whether they live in Ottawa or Iqaluit. This form of uniform delivered pricing is called:
questions.explanation: Single-zone (postage-stamp) pricing charges all buyers the same delivered price, like a stamp that costs the same to mail anywhere - a variation of uniform delivered pricing. Multiple-zone pricing would set different prices for different geographic zones.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a variation of uniform delivered pricing?
questions.explanation: FOB origin pricing is the opposite of uniform delivered pricing - the buyer pays freight from the seller's location. Single-zone, multiple-zone, FOB with freight-allowed (freight absorption) and basing-point pricing are all variations of uniform delivered pricing.

questions.stem: Executives from three Ontario bakeries meet secretly and agree to raise the wholesale price of a loaf of bread by $1.50 at the same time. This is:
questions.explanation: Competitors colluding or conspiring to set prices is price fixing; because the conspirators are rivals at the same level of the channel, it is HORIZONTAL price fixing. Vertical price fixing involves a manufacturer controlling the prices its own resellers charge.

questions.stem: BlendPro, a kitchen-appliance maker, tells retailers they must sell its blenders for no less than $199 and stops shipping to a Winnipeg store that advertised them at $159. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: When a manufacturer controls the resale price its retailers charge, it is vertical price fixing (resale price maintenance), restricted under the Competition Act. Horizontal price fixing would require competing firms at the same level to collude.

questions.stem: Discount Electronics Depot advertises a 65-inch TV for $299 but keeps only one in stock. When shoppers arrive, staff say it is sold out, criticize the model anyway and push an $899 TV instead. This practice is:
questions.explanation: Bait and switch is a form of deceptive pricing: advertising a bargain the seller does not intend to sell, then steering buyers to a pricier item. A genuine loss leader is actually available at the low price to draw traffic.

questions.stem: A shopper at a Halifax hardware store finds a drill with two price stickers: $89.99 and $119.99. Under Canada's rules on double ticketing, what price must the store charge?
options: The average of the two prices
Whatever price is in the store's computer system
questions.explanation: Double ticketing is a deceptive pricing practice; when a product carries two prices, the seller must sell it at the LOWER price. The store cannot charge the higher sticker or default to its system price.

questions.stem: Which situation is price discrimination rather than price fixing?
options: Two competing cement makers agree to charge contractors the same high price
Rival airlines agree to add identical fuel surcharges
A manufacturer charges a large chain a lower price than competing small retailers for the same quantity, lessening competition
Three gas stations in a town agree not to undercut one another
questions.explanation: Price discrimination is one seller charging COMPETING buyers different prices for like quantities in a way that lessens competition. Price fixing is competitors colluding to set prices, as in the other three options.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a form of deceptive pricing?
questions.explanation: Predatory pricing - a very low price set to drive competitors out of business - is a separate legal issue, not deceptive pricing. Bait and switch, double ticketing, bargains conditional on other purchases and misleading comparable-value or suggested-price comparisons are all deceptive pricing.

questions.stem: In Canada, pricing practices such as price fixing and deceptive pricing are governed by the _____, which is enforced by the Competition Bureau.
questions.explanation: The Competition Act, enforced by the Competition Bureau, covers price fixing, price discrimination, deceptive pricing and predatory pricing. The Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act governs the information on labels, not pricing conduct.

questions.stem: When an independent pharmacy opens in a small Alberta town, a national chain drops prices at its nearby store far below cost, planning to raise them again once the independent closes. This is:
questions.explanation: Predatory pricing charges a very low price to injure or drive out competitors, with the plan of raising prices afterward. Loss-leader pricing also cuts prices, but to draw traffic for other products - not to eliminate a rival.
